name: Indus Valley People
desc: Builders of planned cities of baked brick, with straight streets, covered drains in every lane and bathrooms in most houses. They used one standard of weights from Afghanistan to Gujarat, carved tiny seals with unicorns, and wrote in a script no one can yet read.
source: Excavations at Harappa (from 1921), Mohenjo-daro (from 1922), Dholavira, Lothal and Rakhigarhi; Mehrgarh for the older farming villages

cautious: laid a whole street of drains with bricks of the same size
devout: carved a unicorn seal so small it fit on a thumbnail
gluttonous: spun enough cotton thread in a season to dress the whole family

inventions.name: Covered Drains
inventions.source: Mohenjo-daro had brick drains under every street, with inspection holes, and bathrooms with private wells in most houses
inventions.desc: Brick channels under the lanes carry the waste away: the sick recover 20% faster, +1 mood.

inventions.name: Standard Baked Bricks
inventions.source: Indus bricks were made everywhere in the same proportions, 1 : 2 : 4
inventions.desc: Bricks fired hard in kilns, all of the same shape, so any builder can work with any other: building is 12% faster.
inventions.hint: Needs fire and pottery, and builders at the kiln.

inventions.name: Cube Weights
inventions.source: Cubes of polished chert in a fixed series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, then 160, 200...) used across the whole civilisation
inventions.desc: Little stone cubes, doubling in weight, the same in every city: the stores hold 15 more, +1 mood.

inventions.name: Unicorn Seals
inventions.source: Thousands of square steatite seals, most showing a one-horned animal and a line of the undeciphered Indus script
inventions.desc: Tiny carved stamps to seal bales and jars, each with a beast and a few signs: a little more lore, and food spoils 5% slower.

inventions.name: Etched Carnelian Beads
inventions.source: Long carnelian beads, drilled with stone drills and etched white with soda, were traded as far as the Royal Tombs of Ur
inventions.desc: Red stones heated until they glow, drilled for days, and etched with white patterns: +2 mood, and trade brings a little lore.

foods.name: Sesame Cakes
foods.source: Charred sesame seeds from Harappa are among the oldest evidence of the crop
foods.desc: Sesame seeds pounded with jaggery into little cakes: +2 mood, hunger grows 5% slower.

foods.name: Ghee
foods.source: Zebu cattle were domesticated in the Indus region by about 7000 BCE (Mehrgarh)
foods.desc: Butter from zebu milk, simmered clear so it keeps for months in the heat: food spoils 10% slower, hunger grows 5% slower.

finds.name: Tree Cotton
finds.source: Cotton fibres from Mehrgarh (c. 5000 BCE) are the oldest known; Indus cloth was traded to Mesopotamia
finds.desc: Shrubs whose pods burst into soft white fibre. Once known, cotton cloth makes the cold bite 8% less.

finds.name: Carnelian Pebbles
finds.desc: Orange-red pebbles that glow deep red when heated.

people.name: Moha
people.desc: He lays out a new quarter with a cord and a pole before the first brick is set.
memory: laid out the streets of the lower town straight from north to south

people.name: Sindha
people.desc: Her drills of hard stone bore through carnelian a finger-length at a time.
memory: drilled a bead so long it took a whole season

people.name: The Priest-King
people.source: Steatite bust from Mohenjo-daro, c. 2000 BCE (National Museum of Pakistan)
people.desc: A bearded man with a cloak of trefoil patterns and half-closed eyes; no one knows if he was a priest, a king, or neither.

people.name: The Dancing Girl
people.source: Bronze figurine from Mohenjo-daro, c. 2300 BCE (National Museum, New Delhi)
people.desc: A young woman with a hand on her hip and an arm full of bangles, cast by the lost-wax method: one of the oldest bronze sculptures.

people.name: Lu-Enlil
people.source: Indus weights and seals have been found on the island of Dilmun (Bahrain), a hub of the Gulf trade
people.text: a merchant from the islands of the western gulf, who wants beads and cotton and pays in copper and dates.
memory: sailed from Dilmun to the mouth of the great river with a hold full of copper
people.desc: A Gulf merchant of the kind who carried Indus goods to Sumer.

people.name: Ralu
people.label: Ralu, Builder of the Great Bath
people.desc: She makes a pool of brick that does not leak a drop. Crafting 8.

people.name: Kedu
people.label: Kedu, Reader of the Signs
people.desc: The one person who can read every seal. Lore 8.

people.name: Mahal
people.label: Mahal, Captain of the River Boats
people.desc: He takes the boats from the mountains to the sea. Foraging 6, Trade 7.

events.title: The Eastern River Dries
events.source: As the monsoon weakened after about 2200 BCE, the Ghaggar-Hakra river dwindled and people moved east and south into smaller villages
events.text: The river east of the city flows less each year. The elders argue: dig deep wells and hold on, or move toward the rivers of the east, where the rains still come.

options.label: Dig deeper wells
options.result: Brick-lined wells go down, deeper than ever. The city holds on.

options.label: Move east
options.result: Families pack their carts and walk toward the green east.

events.title: A Pool for Purity
events.source: The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, sealed with bitumen and fine brick, perhaps for ritual washing
events.text: The priests ask for a great pool in the heart of the citadel, sealed so tightly that not a drop leaks, where the people can wash themselves clean before the gods.

options.label: Build the Great Bath
options.result: Steps lead down into still water. People come from every quarter to wash on the holy days.

options.label: Wells are enough
options.result: The priests wash at the wells like everyone else.

events.title: Ships for the Far West
events.source: Akkadian texts speak of ships of Meluhha (the Indus) bringing carnelian, ivory and timber to Mesopotamia
events.text: Sailors say there is a land far to the west, at the head of the gulf, where kings pay anything for red beads. A ship could go, if the tribe can fill it.

options.label: Send the ship
options.result: The ship returns with copper, silver and strange stories of cities of mud.

options.label: Keep the beads
options.result: The beads stay on our own necks.

tales.name: The One-Horned Beast
tales.source: A story made up around the unicorn seals
tales.text: In the forests at the edge of the world lives a beast with one horn, which no one has ever caught. It comes to drink only from water that is clean. That is why we carve it on our seals: it means what is inside is honest, and the water of our city is pure.

tales.name: The Lord of the Beasts
tales.source: A story made up around the 'Pashupati' seal of Mohenjo-daro, a horned figure seated among animals
tales.text: A great one sits with his legs folded, wearing horns, and around him stand the tiger, the elephant, the rhinoceros and the buffalo, and two deer lie at his feet. None of them harms another while he sits there. When the herders take the cattle out, they ask him to keep the tigers calm.

tales.name: Why Our Streets Run Straight
tales.source: A story made up around the grid plans of Indus cities
tales.text: When the first city was built, every family wanted its house to face the river. They quarrelled until the wisest woman drew lines in the sand with a cord: north to south, east to west. 'Now no house is better than another,' she said, 'and every drain runs to the river.'

tales.name: The Bathing Day
tales.source: A story made up around the Great Bath
tales.text: On the bathing day the whole city climbs to the citadel in clean cotton, and one by one the people go down the brick steps into the still water. They come up laughing, with flowers in their hair, and the drums play in the courtyard until the stars come out.
